content: What is the current process state? Report commanded and measured X position, Y position, laser power, and scan speed, including units and anomaly evaluation status.

**Current Process State**

| Metric | Commanded | Measured | Units | Anomaly Evaluation |
|--------|-----------|----------|-------|--------------------|
| X position | **‑5.19** | **‑5.1453** | mm | **Normal** (difference = ‑0.045 mm, within the 0.25 mm threshold) |
| Y position | **16.0** | **15.845** | mm | **Normal** (difference = +0.155 mm, within the 0.25 mm threshold) |
| Laser power | **100.0** | **0.0** | W | **Anomaly** (difference = 100 W, exceeds the 10 W threshold) |
| Scan speed | **900.0** | **947.0** | mm/s | **Not evaluated** (no threshold configured) |

All values are taken directly from the latest system readout.
What do the current laser-power and melt-pool measurements show? Report the available values with units and distinguish missing measurements from zero values.

**Laser‑power measurement**  
- Measured laser power: **0.0 W** – this is a reported zero value (the sensor is providing a reading of zero, not a missing value).

**Melt‑pool measurements** (all reported as zero values)  
- Melt‑pool length (t = 100 %): **0.0 mm**  
- Melt‑pool width (t = 100 %): **0.0 mm**  
- Melt‑pool area at 80 % threshold: **0.0 mm²**  
- Melt‑pool area at 100 % threshold: **0.0 mm²**  
- Melt‑pool area at 120 % threshold: **0.0 mm²**

All of the above values are present and are zero; no measurements are missing.
Does the zero laser-power reading prove a hardware failure or a defective part? Explain possible causes and what additional evidence would be needed to distinguish them

**Zero‑power reading – hardware failure or part defect?** | Possibility | Why it could produce a zero‑power reading | What extra evidence is needed to tell which one it is | |-------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------| | **Hardware failure** (laser, power supply, or power‑sensor fault) | * The DAQ reports **0 W** while the XYPT command is 100 W, indicating the laser never delivered optical power.
* The melt‑pool dimensions are all **0**, consistent with no laser‑induced melt.
* The anomaly detector flags the laser‑power metric as an **anomaly** (difference = 100 W > 10 W threshold). | • **Measured laser‑power trace** from the DAQ over the full scan (does it stay at 0 W for the entire track or only at the start?).
• **XYPT power channel** (the command side) to confirm the command was actually sent and not suppressed by a higher‑level safety interlock.
• **Laser‑status diagnostics** (e.g., diode current, fault flags, power‑supply voltage) from the machine controller.
• **Camera or photodiode view** of the spot (visible‑light or infrared) to see whether any light is emitted when the laser should be on.
• **System log messages** indicating laser‑startup errors or interlock trips. | | **Defective part / process condition** (e.g., the part geometry or powder condition causes the control system to shut the laser off) | * Some LPBF controllers disable the laser when an abnormal condition is detected (e.g., excessive spatter, loss of focus, safety‑zone violation). The command may still be 100 W, but the controller forces the output to 0 W.
* If the part’s overhang or powder condition caused a sensor to think the laser was out of range, the controller could have aborted the melt, leaving the melt‑pool measurements at zero. | • **Control‑system status flags** that indicate an “laser‑off” event triggered by a process‑monitoring rule (e.g., spike in acoustic signal, camera‑based plume detection).
• **Layer‑wise imaging** showing whether the scan line was actually written (the image would be blank if no melt occurred).
• **Powder‑bed or part‑inspection data** that could explain a deliberate laser shutdown (e.g., detected powder depletion, part‑collision warning).
• **Comparison with previous builds** of the same part: if only this build shows zero power while others show normal power, the cause is more likely a part‑specific safety trigger. | ### Bottom line The present data (command = 100 W, measured = 0 W, melt‑pool = 0) **confirms an anomaly** but does **not by itself prove whether the cause is a hardware fault or a part‑related safety shutdown**. To distinguish the two, you need **additional diagnostics** such as: 1. Real‑time power traces from both the command (XYPT) and measurement (DAQ) channels. 2. Laser‑status or fault registers from the controller. 3. Optical/infrared camera images of the scan track during the build. 4. Log entries or interlock messages that indicate a forced laser‑off event. 5. Comparison with earlier or subsequent builds to see if the zero‑power condition is repeatable. Collecting and reviewing those pieces of evidence will allow you to attribute the zero‑power reading to either a hardware malfunction or a process‑safety response triggered by the part or powder condition.
What should the operator check next before changing any process settings? Base your guidance on the available evidence and state what remains uncertain.

**What the operator should check next (before touching any process parameters)** | Step | Why it matters (based on the data you have) | How to do it | |------|--------------------------------------------|--------------| | 1. **Verify the laser‑control status** | The DAQ reports **0 W** while the command is 100 W and the anomaly detector flags laser‑power as an *anomaly*. This could be a hardware fault **or** an automatic “laser‑off” safety trigger. | – Open the machine‑controller UI or console and look for laser‑status flags (e.g., *Laser Ready*, *Fault*, *Interlock*).
– Read any fault codes or warnings in the system log that were generated in the last few seconds. | | 2. **Confirm that the command is actually reaching the laser** | The “command” value (100 W) comes from the XYPT file, but the controller might have suppressed the output. | – Check the XYPT command channel (or the “laser‑trigger” line) in the DAQ to see the **commanded power waveform** during the current scan.
– Compare it to the measured power trace; if the command trace also drops to 0 W, the issue is upstream (software/safety). | | 3. **Inspect the power‑measurement sensor and wiring** | A faulty power sensor could report 0 W even if the laser is on. | – Look at the sensor status LEDs (if any) and verify connector integrity.
– Run a quick calibration or self‑test (many systems have a “sensor test” routine). | | 4. **Look at the coaxial melt‑pool camera or infrared view** | All melt‑pool geometry values are 0 mm, which is consistent with *no* laser light reaching the powder. A live camera image will instantly tell you whether a melt track is being generated. | – Open the real‑time camera feed for the current layer.
– If the spot is completely dark, the laser is off; if a bright spot is visible but the power reading is 0 W, the sensor is likely faulty. | | 5. **Check safety interlocks and environmental alarms** | The controller may have disabled the laser because of gas‑flow, oxygen‑level, or enclosure‑door faults. | – Review the “environment” panel for oxygen ppm, gas‑flow, door‑open, or pressure‑relief alarms. | | 6. **Review recent layer‑wise imaging** (if available) | Layer‑wise images will show whether material was actually fused on the previous layers. | – Browse the most recent layer images; a completely blank image indicates no melt. | | 7. **Physical inspection (quick)** | A hot laser diode or audible humming can be a quick sanity check. | – Carefully feel (or listen for) the laser head; it should be warm and emit a faint hum when powered. **Do not touch the optics directly.** | --- ### What still remains uncertain | Unknown | What could be causing it | Evidence needed | |--------|---------------------------|-----------------| | **Is the laser hardware actually off?** | – Fault in laser diode / power supply
– Interlock that forced a shutdown | • Laser‑status flags or fault codes
• Real‑time camera/IR view showing no spot | | **Is the power‑measurement sensor broken?** | – Sensor disconnected or saturated
– Calibration error | • Sensor self‑test / calibration result
• Comparison of command vs. measured waveform | | **Did the control software deliberately suppress power because of a safety rule?** | – Excessive spatter, out‑of‑range plume, powder‑bed issue detected by onboard analytics | • Log entries indicating “laser off due to safety condition”
• Safety‑rule status panel | | **Is the part or powder condition causing an automatic shutdown?** | – Powder depletion, over‑exposure, or geometry that triggered a protection | • Powder‑bed inspection or recent powder‑replenishment record
• Part‑specific warnings in the log | --- ### Immediate recommendation 1. **Do not change any laser‑power, scan‑speed, or positional set‑points yet.** 2. Follow the checklist above, starting with the **laser‑status / fault log** and the **real‑time camera view**, because these give the fastest indication of whether the laser is truly off. 3. Once you have confirmed whether the laser is physically off **or** the sensor is at fault, you can decide whether a hardware repair, sensor recalibration, or a safety‑interlock reset is required before resuming or adjusting the process.
